Potatoes ‘boil’ in the ground as record heatwave sweeps across swathes of Asia
South Korean farmers are suffering in record heat, as Hong Kong reports its highest ever temperature and Japan swelters through newly designated ‘cruelly hot’ days
In a potato field in Yanggu county, 80 miles (130km) north-east of Seoul, Lee Sang-hyuk dug into the soil and found nothing worth saving.
A week earlier the crop, located in Gangwon province, had looked fine. Now the potatoes came up soft and collapsing, “like boiled potatoes”, spoiled by heat that had turned the ground into something closer to an oven.
“It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” he told local broadcaster SBS.
His ruined harvest is one thread in a punishing summer across east Asia, as record heat swept through South Korea, Japan and Hong Kong in recent weeks.
On 2 August, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5C, the highest registered in South Korea since modern weather observations began in 1904.
The heat has since been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to the country’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have died.
Authorities issued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, told his cabinet the extreme weather was “unlike anything we have experienced before”.
“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system,” he said, “since this extreme weather is becoming the new normal.”
In neighbouring Japan, temperatures reached 40C or higher at multiple locations and the country recorded its first ever “kokushobi”, or “cruelly hot day”, a new category introduced this year by the country’s weather agency for temperatures above 40C. In Tokyo, three lions died of suspected heatstroke at a city zoo.
Scientists say the extremes are part of a wider pattern. Researchers working through Japan’s Weather Attribution Centre found that the country’s intense July heat would have been “virtually impossible” without global warming.
Without the warming caused by human activity, they calculated, a heatwave of this scale would occur on average once ever 10,000 years.
The heat struck even as an El Niño event was under way, a natural climate pattern that has in the past been associated with a lower likelihood of extreme summer heat in Japan.
In Hong Kong, its observatory posted an official temperature of 36.9C, the highest recorded there since records began in 1884, as the outer bands of Typhoon Dolphin swept hot air over the city.
The record heat also exposed the failings of the city’s heat stress warning system for outdoor workers, which remained at its lowest tier even as temperatures reached a record high.
“The threshold for the red warning is clearly set too high”, Lam Chiu Ying, a former head of the Hong Kong Observatory, wrote on Facebook. “If even a record-breaking temperature can’t trigger it, isn’t it just a display piece used to decorate a shop window?”
Hong Kong’s Labour Department has since said it is reviewing the warning system with the observatory.
In China’s western Xinjiang region, a weather station recorded a 50C reading in July and heatwaves gripped the country’s north-east, while North Korea reported a run of tropical nights in Pyongyang, with temperatures failing to fall below 25C.
June-Yi Lee, a climate scientist at Pusan National University and a coordinating lead author of the UN’s most recent climate assessment, said the regional heatwave may have been shaped by a mix of atmospheric circulation patterns and a warming climate.
A strengthening ridge of high pressure over the Tibetan Plateau and western Pacific, layered on top of this year’s El Niño, may have helped create conditions for the heat, she said.
The World Meteorological Organization said in its latest State of the Climate in Asia report that the pace of Asia’s warming between 1991 and 2025 is roughly twice that of the preceding three decades.
About 160 miles (257km) south of Seoul, in Gwangju, watermelon farmer Hong Kyung-hee watched fruit that would normally sell at a premium turn to mush.
“The inside was good, the sweetness was good, everything was fine”, he told KBS from his farm. “But after three days it changed overnight like this. In my 50 years of farming, this is the first time.”
Strawberry farmer Yoon Woo-ha in Damyang county, South Jeolla province, lost seedlings that she had cultivated for three months and won’t be covered by insurance.
South Korea’s crop insurance scheme covers only designated crops, growing methods and regions, leaving farmers exposed when losses fall outside those boundaries.
“When the insurance can’t cover this,” said Lee Jun-kyung, head of the Gwangju chapter of the Korean Peasants League, “it goes straight into farm household debt.”
Prof Lee warned that heatwaves were expected to become more frequent and intense as the climate heated up, while compound extremes, such as consecutive heatwaves and heavy rainfall, were becoming more common.
“There is an urgent need for rapid, large-scale reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to limit further global warming together with well-planned adaptation measures to address the climate change that is already occurring,” she said.

What is marine heatwave? Know how superheated oceans can harm human health
What is marine heatwave? Know how superheated oceans can harm human health
Marine heatwaves occur when ocean temperatures stay unusually high for prolonged periods, disrupting ecosystems and potentially affecting human health through heat exposure, seafood risks and air quality.
Marine heatwaves are not solely an environmental issue impacting the marine biota and coral reefs. Researchers say that extended periods of unusually warm ocean conditions can also impact human health, food security, livelihoods and mental health. A team of researchers from Adelaide University and the University of Hong Kong have published a paper in Nature Sustainability that addresses marine heatwaves. It also stresses the chain reaction they can reach to coastal communities and people who rely on the ocean.
What is a marine heatwave?
A marine heat wave is defined as when sea surface temperatures are higher than usual for that time and place for an extended period of time. According to scientists these events may impact large populations and marine ecosystems. They have been associated with coral bleaching, widespread deaths of marine organisms, harmful algal blooms (HABs) and significant disturbances in fisheries and aquaculture.
As global temperatures rise experts suggest that the frequency, length and severity of marine heatwaves may increase by reaching greater intensity. This implies that their impacts may extend beyond the ocean and pose a threat to human populations.
How can marine heatwaves impact human health?
Researchers have discovered several direct and indirect impacts of marine heatwaves on humans. According to the findings warm ocean temperatures can fuel storms and other extreme events. This may result in injuries, fatalities, uprooting and destruction of houses and property. For instance, Hurricane Otis in 2013 was unusually warm and rapidly strengthened seawater in Mexico which triggered estimated damages of US$15 billion. Whereas Typhoon Doksuri which has been linked to exceptionally warm ocean waters impacted over 2 million people in Asia in 2023.
Is seafood safe during marine heatwaves?
The team of researchers claim that there is a major concern about the impacts of marine heatwaves on seafood safety and availability. Researchers note that warm waters can lead to blooms of algae that can produce toxins making seafood dangerous to human health. Marine heatwaves can also impact fisheries and aquaculture activities by impacting seafood production and community livelihoods that depend on the ocean for their food and livelihoods. In addition experts caution that such weather conditions can be a food security issue particularly for those who rely on seafood as a primary source of food.
Could marine heatwaves impact mental wellbeing?
What is more concerning about this study is that scientists point out that marine heatwaves may also manifest in mental health. Individuals with strong ties to the ocean including those whose living activities, cultural practices and play are tied to the sea might suffer from emotional hardship when the marine ecosystem is degraded. Possible outcomes of repeated environmental damage are highlighted as anxiety, grief, frustration and depression. Eco anxiety and emotional struggles as well as physical health issues like respiratory irritation and asthma were also linked to the toxic algal bloom in 2025 in South Australia.

The authors suggest that governments and public health organisations should take account of marine heatwave predictions in their health emergency preparedness. Improved collaboration among ocean researchers, health officials, and coastal resource managers may also enable communities to be more proactive in their response to events.

Country diary: This is how bad the heatwave has got for us arable farmers – I’m going on holiday
Brigg, Lincolnshire: I should be busy, but the boom-bust climate has upset all my usual routines
By the time you read this, I will be away in the Scottish Borders – a British arable farmer on holiday in August? This is unheard of. I’ve never done it myself in 30 years of farming. The reason I’m going away is that, remarkably, I have very little to do, and it’s all down to this destructive modern climate.
We have finished the harvest, all done in almost entirely the month of July. Overall our farm will be 20% down on our long-term average yield, with winter cropping 2 tonnes per hectare and spring cropping 1 tonne per hectare below normal. Winter barley will be the only crop close to normal yields due to its natural maturity at the time of the first heatwave in late May. Beans finished five weeks ahead of schedule, and are almost 50% down on expectations.
So, what to do? Normally I would be drilling cover crops and soon oilseed rape, but there is no point – the soil is just too dry. Instead, I’m doing odd jobs like digging up “blown” land drains (bursts in the piping deep underground that is the backbone of our healthy soils).
Meanwhile, traditional hedgerow plants such as blackberries have appeared early, and I worry for the wildlife (which seem to have a decent number of young this year) if winter is prolonged.
The heat will make the headlines, but only a few months ago the farm was suffering from excess rainfall. This, I feel, has done more harm to our crops than the high temperatures, as the clay loam here can tolerate dryness to some extent.
The new normal is all boom and bust: long spells of either extreme, with little in the way of typical seasonal weather, making growing any form of food challenging. Some think we can import our way out of this problem, yet the UK is not alone in having such issues.
So for now it is a bit of rest, but as the season changes I will be back to do what we do best: grow the nation’s food. If the climate lets us.

The RCN said heatwaves were making some settings “impossible and inhumane” places to work and receive care in, and it called for buildings to be “heat-proofed” by air conditioning if necessary.
It said facilities too often have windows that do not open, and criticised a widespread lack of air conditioning, fans or ventilation, run by NHS managers who reject requests and refuse to relax dress codes.
The college said nursing staff were “dripping with sweat from head to toe” and that one nurse had been admitted to the hospital where she worked after collapsing from dehydration.
Temperatures reaching 36C
Two nurses with pre-existing conditions told the union they had suffered seizures as a result of working in hot environments.
Meanwhile, a number of pregnant nurses complained about the impact of working in temperatures up to 32C on their and their babies’ health.
One nurse said they felt “nauseous, dizzy and faint” after temperatures exceeded 33C, while a nurse working in a Welsh endoscopy ward said their room reached 35C after its air conditioning unit broke.
One staff member in an English hospital said they were told they could not use fans or air conditioning units because of “limitations with the wing’s electrical supply”.
Another said staff had been given “an old and faulty air conditioning unit that was actually raising the temperature in the clinic room”.
One nurse working in “excessive heat” said managers had blocked the use of cooling systems and not conducted a risk assessment of caring for elderly patients in temperatures that had reached 36C.
Another said: “We have elderly patients in our clinic, who we are increasingly worried about. We have got to the end of our tether with no support from our immediate seniors.”
Staff also reported that patients were having to wait and recover from surgery in hot rooms, with one member saying they had “formally requested air con units as both staff and patients are suffering”.
Other staff said medication trolleys had to be “taken to the coolest building to ensure the medications retained their efficacy”, while dialysis machines had to be removed to stop them overheating.
Last month, the Telegraph revealed that blood tests had been cancelled because the NHS was unable to prevent test tubes and samples from being degraded by the heat.
Prof Nicola Ranger, the RCN’s general secretary and chief executive, said that employers had a legal duty to make the workplace safe, which included “installing air conditioning, improving ventilation, ensuring water and heat-appropriate uniforms are available and guaranteeing risk assessments are a core part of business planning, especially for pregnant or vulnerable workers”.
She added: “When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed.
Ms Cooper said: “The extreme heat is hitting public health and our NHS. Across the NHS and social care, staff are doing a remarkable job to respond to rising A&E attendances and ambulance call outs, heat problems amongst the elderly and difficult working conditions. I want to thank them for all their work.

DH reminds public to take precautions against heat-related illnesses during very hot weather
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) today (August 13) reminded members of the public to take appropriate precautions against heat-related illnesses, such as heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, during very hot weather.
The Centre for Health Protection, Photo source: reference image
In a high-temperature environment, excessive sweating and difficulty in heat dissipation can cause stress to the body. Members of the public should take the following precautions:
- Hydrate in a timely manner to prevent dehydration;
- Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting and breathable clothing to minimise heat absorption and facilitate perspiration and heat dissipation;
- Keep indoor areas well ventilated and maintain appropriate temperature and humidity, e.g. by opening windows or using a fan or air-conditioning;
- Avoid strenuous exercise and prolonged activities such as hiking or trekking;
- Arrange outdoor activities in the morning or the late afternoon, if possible, and bring enough water; and
- Avoid beverages containing caffeine, such as coffee and tea, as well as alcoholic beverages, which may speed up water loss through the urinary system.
In addition, infants and children, the elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses such as heart disease or high blood pressure, overweight people and outdoor/manual workers are more susceptible to heat stroke. These groups should pay special attention to the following:
- Infants and young children: Avoid going outside when the temperature is high. If they must go outside, adults should ensure they stay in places with moderate temperatures and good ventilation or air-conditioning. Infants and young children should never be left unattended in a confined space such as a vehicle;
- The elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses and overweight people: Pay close attention to health conditions and seek help as soon as possible if experiencing any abnormalities in health indicators such as blood pressure, heart rate, etc or if there are fluctuations in health conditions. Avoid going out when the temperature is high. Make sure there is good ventilation, or turn on a fan or air-conditioner to keep an appropriate temperature indoors. High temperatures can also worsen the condition of people with chronic illnesses (such as cardiovascular and respiratory diseases). Therefore, they should have an ample supply of their usual medication and keep in contact with family members, neighbours and the community. People should seek immediate help if they feel unwell.
- Outdoor/manual workers: Reschedule work to cooler hours as far as feasible. If working in a hot environment is unavoidable, provide shade where practicable and use ventilation and heat dissipation equipment. Once work has begun, gradually adjust the pace of work and take breaks in the shade to regain strength.
The DH reminded the public that heat stroke is one of the most common health risks in hot weather. Over the past five years, there have been over 200 hospital admissions due to heat stroke each year in Hong Kong, with two to five fatal cases occurring mainly during the summer months from May to September. Vulnerable groups are more susceptible to heat stroke. Symptoms include dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion. In severe cases, patients may suffer from convulsions or become unconscious, which can be life-threatening if they are not cooled down and resuscitated in a timely manner.
Members of the public are also advised to pay attention to the latest weather, as well as the real-time and forecasted ultraviolet (UV) index released by the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO). When the UV index is high (6 or above), the public should note the following:
- Avoid direct sunlight exposure to the skin and the eyes;
- Apply broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen liberally, with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 30 or higher, when participating in outdoor activities. Reapply every two hours if staying outdoors for long periods, or after swimming, sweating or towelling off;
- While using DEET-containing insect repellents for personal protection against mosquito-borne diseases, apply sunscreen before insect repellent;
If symptoms develop, such as dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion, rest and seek help immediately, and seek medical advice as soon as possible.
For more health information, the public may visit the CHP's heat stroke page and UV radiation page; the HKO's Dial-a-Weather (1878 200), latest weather report and forecast, UV Index and weather information for hiking and mountaineering; and press releases of the Labour Department on precautions against heat stroke for outdoor workers and their employers when the Heat Stress at Work Warning is in force.

Mainland flagship game developer S-GAME establishes Hong Kong base to drive global launch of AAA title Phantom Blade Zero
Invest Hong Kong today (August 13) announced that S-GAME, a leading Chinese Mainland game and content developer, has established a new Hong Kong office dedicated to game publishing and distribution, promotion, trading, and cross-media intellectual property (IP) business. Using Hong Kong as its base, the company will drive the overseas expansion of its soon-to-be-launched AAA martial-arts action game Phantom Blade Zero.
Hailed as the most anticipated Chinese AAA game of 2026, Phantom Blade Zero has attracted keen attention from players worldwide. The martial-arts action title blends Eastern wuxia elements with dark fantasy aesthetics to form its distinctive "Kungfupunk" style. Phantom Blade Zero's art centre is also based in Hong Kong, with the art team bringing together creative talent from across Greater China. Several veteran Hong Kong film martial-arts choreographers took part in the game's action production, and as a result, the high-speed combat and action design within the game are rich with the flavour of Hong Kong's martial-arts cinema. The game opened for global pre-order starting yesterday (August 12). In its latest trailer, S-GAME announced that renowned Hong Kong kung fu film star and director Donnie Yen has served as the Creative Consultant of Phantom Blade Zero since 2023, and personally performed both the motion captures and facial captures for a major in-game character, "Mó Yuan". The game is scheduled to launch worldwide simultaneously on Steam, Epic Games Store, and PlayStation on October 29 this year.
Associate Director-General of Investment Promotion Mr Arnold Lau said, "China is not only a vast IP consumer market, but has also become a globally recognised base for creative exports. As a hub connecting the world, Hong Kong, with its mature professional services, bilingual talent, media networks and a robust intellectual property protection regime, will provide crucial support for S-GAME's overseas distribution and IP internationalisation. Meanwhile, Phantom Blade Zero has drawn on Hong Kong's rich pool of international film talent and resources, fusing the martial-arts aesthetics of classic Hong Kong cinema into a next-generation video game, achieving cross-border and cross-media cultural inheritance. We look forward to enterprises leveraging Hong Kong as a base for global promotion so that outstanding works can extend their influence far and wide."
The Marketing Director of S-GAME, Mr Julius Li, said, "Hong Kong is the natural choice for S-GAME's journey into international markets. Hong Kong is not only a top-tier global financial and business centre, but also a storied hub for international film and publishing - an inspiration for Phantom Blade Zero and a strategic vantage point for taking 'Kungfupunk' game culture global. The talent, legal and business environment, media influence and urban culture here all meet our global distribution needs and align closely with the creative roots of Phantom Blade Zero. The newly established Hong Kong office will support us in advancing international business liaisons, international advertising, IP licensing, as well as the possible future production and distribution of film and television spin-offs, bringing this work rooted in the East onto the world stage."
S-GAME was founded by Mr Liang Qiwei (Soulframe) in 2011, with original IPs including the Rainblood series and the Phantom Blade series of mobile games. Phantom Blade Zero, the title being launched, drew an enthusiastic response at a large-scale offline trial event held in Beijing in July 2025, capturing the attention of players at home and abroad, with cumulative views surpassing 100 million and livestream viewership exceeding 20 million.
For more information about Phantom Blade Zero, please visit pbz.s-game.cn.

UK could see hottest day of year as parts of England may hit 38C
Rare amber ‘extreme heat’ warnings have been issued by the Met Office from 9am to midnight on Thursday.
Bookmark
Bookmark popover
Removed from bookmarks
The UK could see its hottest day of the year so far as parts of England may hit 38C during the peak of the fifth heatwave of the summer.
Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings have been issued by the Met Office for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of the Government’s emergency Cobra committee on Wednesday in response to the prolonged spell of exceptionally hot and dry weather.
Met Office forecaster Alex Burkill said: “Temperatures (in areas covered by the amber warning) could reach highs of around 36, 37, possibly 38C.
“Now when you get these sorts of high temperatures, well that’s when we could see impacts to our infrastructure, our railway lines, our roads, they are not designed for this sort of heat.
“And more people are likely to be impacted by how hot it is with regards to their health.”
He added: “It could be the hottest day of the year so far if we get above 38C, and if we get above 38.5C, well it could be the hottest August day on record, but that’s actually pretty unlikely.”
The highest temperature of the year was 38C recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on June 28.
It comes as England and Wales have already seen as many wildfires this year as in the whole of 2025.
Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), the same as last year’s record-breaking total.
Crews from Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service have continued battling a blaze which hit protected heathland in the New Forest after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood on Sunday.
In an update on Wednesday evening, the fire service said crews expect to be at the scene for at least another three to four days.
Most major UK supermarkets have stopped sales of disposable barbecues in recent weeks in line with voluntary guidance from the NFCC.
Mr Burnham has urged all shops to stop selling them and indicated that an outright ban could be considered in future summers.
The Prime Minister also said that there had been a “significant number of excess deaths from heat this summer already” and urged the public to follow health advice, including checking in on elderly friends and relatives.
Two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.
The Royal College of Nursing has warned that nurses are collapsing at work and are being forced to care for patients in temperatures in excess of 30C.
Others have reported seizures and “dripping with sweat from head to toe”, and nurses have said patients are being cared for in hospitals which have been described as “unbearably hot” and “not fit for humans”.
Nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.
Baroness Brown, who chairs the independent advisory Climate Change Committee’s adaptation work, warned it “gets worse from here” until the greenhouse gas emissions – mostly caused by burning fossil fuels in power plants, vehicles, home heating and industry – behind global warming are cut to zero overall, known as net zero.
Meanwhile, Chiltern Railways and East Midlands Railway have issued alerts to “only travel if essential”.
Other operators will either run a reduced timetable or are warning about the potential for short-notice cancellations.

Gujarat received widespread rainfall over the past 24 hours, with Khedbrahma in Sabarkantha recording the highest rainfall at 3.27 inches.
Vadgam in Banaskantha recorded 3.11 inches, while six other talukas received more than 2 inches of rain during the period.
The state has so far recorded 3% more rainfall than normal. However, Saurashtra and Kutch continue to face a rainfall deficit, with both regions recording 21% less rain than average.
Elderly man, youth swept into drain in Patan
An elderly man and a youth who rushed to rescue him fell into an open drain on Sidhpur Road in Patan after heavy rain left the busy stretch submerged.
Water accumulated up to knee level from Navjivan Char Rasta, turning the road into a virtual lake and making the uncovered drain difficult to spot.
Youth also fell while attempting rescue
The elderly man suddenly stepped into the open drain after it was concealed by the floodwater. A local youth immediately rushed to help him but also fell into the drain.
People nearby responded quickly and, after considerable effort, pulled both of them out safely. Their timely intervention helped avert a potentially serious incident.
Locals angry over open drain
The incident has triggered strong resentment among residents, who have questioned the municipality’s failure to secure or cover the open drain despite the area being prone to waterlogging.
Locals said, “The submerged road and uncovered drain posed a serious risk to pedestrians and demanded immediate action from the civic authorities.”

Brace for brownouts on Aug. 13, red alert up for Visayas grid
By: Morexette Marie B. Erram - Acting Assistant Business Editor - CDN Digital |August 13,2026 - 09:00 AM
CEBU CITY, Philippines — For the 6th time in a row, the Visayas grid was placed under red alert Thursday, Aug. 13, as available power capacity fell below forecast peak demand.
The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP), in its 8 a.m. advisory, placed available capacity at 2,283 megawatts (MW) against a forecast peak demand of 2,360 MW, a 77-MW shortfall.
The grid was placed under red alert from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m.
Yellow alerts were also declared from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. to 9 p.m.
NGCP attributed the alerts to the continued unavailability of three major coal-fired units in the Visayas as well as reduced power imports from Mindanao.
The reduced imports were partly due to a scheduled maintenance outage at GNPower Kauswagan (GNPK) 2 and an emergency shutdown of GNPK 1 following a boiler tube leak, NGCP said.
High forecast system demand also contributed to the tight supply situation.
The latest alert came as a growing number of generating units remain unavailable across the Visayas grid.
NGCP data showed 27 power plants on forced outage, with six going offline in August, two in July, three in June, seven in May, one in March, three in 2025, two in 2024, two in 2023 and one since 2021.
Another 13 plants were operating at derated capacities.
Together, the forced outages and derations have taken 903.2 MW out of the grid.
Restoring all of this capacity would be more than enough to cover Thursday’s projected 77-MW supply deficit.
A red alert is declared when available supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the regulating reserve required to maintain grid frequency.
A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin falls below the contingency reserve needed to absorb the sudden loss of the largest online generating unit without affecting customers.
